header: Question 10 Dyotropic Rearrangements. A dyotropic rearrangement is a pericyclic isomerization in which two σ bonds migrate simultaneously within a molecule. Type I and type II rearrangements often show good stereoselectivity and can be used in natural-product synthesis.

subquestions.text_open: 10.1 Four-membered-ring lactones are common substrates for dyotropic rearrangements. The following rearrangement constructs a fused lactone containing 3 contiguous stereocenters in one step. 10.1.1 Draw a Newman projection of the reactive conformation of the substrate, viewed along its dashed-wedge bond.

text_images.description: Dynamic rearrangement equilibria labeled type I and type II. Type I shows an open-chain system in which groups A and B are attached to a carbon chain containing unsaturation; dashed lines indicate delocalization or partial double-bond character, and the equilibrium reversibly shifts the unsaturation or conjugated system along the chain while changing molecular configuration. Type II shows a three-dimensional bridged or cage-like polycycle. In the left isomer, A and B lie on a particular front-right C-C single bond and a C=C bond lies at the rear left. Rearrangement breaks the A/B-bearing bond and forms a new A/B-bearing bond at the front left while shifting the double bond concertedly.

Question 10.1: four-membered-ring lactone substrate 'O=C1O[C@@H](C2CCCC2)[C@@H]1OC3=CC=CC=C3' undergoes an MgBr_2-promoted dyotropic rearrangement to give fused lactone '[H]C4(C(C(O5)=O)OC6=CC=CC=C6)C5([H])CCCC4' with 3 contiguous stereocenters.

subquestions.text_open: 10.1.2 Write the product SMILES, including stereochemistry.

10.2 The natural product curcumanolide A can be synthesized concisely through the key steps of the following small-organic-molecule-catalyzed asymmetric intramolecular lactonization and dyotropic rearrangement. 10.2.1 Write the SMILES strings of at least 2 key intermediates in the first transformation.

text_images.description: A multistep synthesis. Reactant 'O=C(CCC1=O)C1(CCCC(O)=O)C' reacts under cat. and a catalyst bearing a dashed-wedge Ph group, SMILES '[C@H]7(CCN8C(SC9=C8C=CC=C9)=N7)C%10=CC=CC=C%10', with TsCl, LiCl, iPr_2NEt below the arrow, to give intermediate 'O=C(O2)[C@H]3CC[C@]4([C@]32CCC4=O)C'. mCPBA then gives A; cat. TMSOTf converts A to B; 2 parallel arrows convert B to curcumanolide A, SMILES 'O=C(/C(C5)=C(C)\C)O[C@]65[C@H](CC[C@H]6C(OC)=O)C'.

subquestions.text_open: 10.2.2 State the role of LiCl in the first transformation.
10.2.3 In a later step, Lewis acid TMSOTf catalyzes dyotropic rearrangement of A to B. Write the SMILES strings of A and B, including stereochemistry.
10.3 Dyotropic rearrangements can also occur at transition metals. Write the SMILES string of intermediate C in the following transformation.

text_images.description: A two-step reaction. A reactant bearing central Cp_2Zr and two furan rings, SMILES 'C1([ZrCp2]C2=CC=CO2)=CC=CO1', is heated at 185 °C to intermediate 'C'. C then reacts with MeO_2C-C≡C-CO_2Me, SMILES 'COC(=O)C#CC(=O)OC', at 105 °C to give a benzene product bearing two methoxycarbonyl groups, CO_2Me, and one furan on three consecutive carbons, SMILES 'COC(=O)C1=C(C(=O)OC)C(C2=CC=CO2)=CC=C1'.

subquestions.text_open: 10.4 Type II dyotropic rearrangements generally require aromatization as a driving force. The following transformation may involve a dyotropic mechanism, so researchers tested it using a deuterated substrate. If the reaction follows a dyotropic mechanism, which positions in the product are deuterated? Circle them on the answer sheet.

text_images.description: A consecutive 2-step reaction. Reactant 'O=C1OC(C2=C1CC3=C(C2)CC3)=O' and deuterated reactant 'C=C4C([2H])C=CC([2H])C4=C', which has 2 wavy bonds labeled D and the English-localized caption 1:1 mixture of cis/trans isomers, are joined by a plus sign and heated at 117 °C to intermediate '[2H]C5C=CC([2H])C6=C5CC(C7)(C(O8)=O)C(C6)(C8=O)CC(C7=C)=C', also bearing 2 wavy D bonds. Heating at 150 °C gives final product 'O=C(O9)C%10%11C(CC(C=CC=C%12)=C%12C%11)(C9=O)CC(C)=C(C)C%10'.
